summary: Brick conical light on a Lake Huron point north of Harrisville, Michigan, built 1869-1870 for a reef; automated 1913; now run by the Alcona Historical Society.

access.note: Lighthouse and museums open to visitors on summer weekends; grounds open all year (Alcona Historical Society; LighthouseFriends).

facts.agency: Michigan Department of Natural Resources (owner, awarded 2005); managed by the Alcona Historical Society

events.note: Congress appropriated the requested $15,000 on 2 March 1867
Tower and dwelling completed early November 1870
Sources differ: the Alcona Historical Society gives spring 1870; LighthouseFriends says the first lighting waited until the spring after completion (1871)
Third-and-a-half-order Henry-Lepaute Fresnel lens (LighthouseFriends). The archive lists the original optic as sixth order.
Life-Saving Station established adjacent to the lighthouse; Station No. 5 in the Life-Saving Service's 1881 report

Steamer Marine City burned in late August 1880. The Life-Saving Service gives 29 August, off Alcona, nine lost; LighthouseFriends gives 28 August, off Sturgeon Point, twenty lost of 160 aboard. The Cheboygan Northern Tribune reported a later 'fifty or sixty' dispatch and then said it proved untrue; a first-person account in the same issue gives eight missing.
Five cribs built along the shore as the lake approached the tower
Lens damaged; the old lens sent to the Staten Island depot for repair (LighthouseFriends)
Brick-lined circular iron oil house built (LighthouseFriends)
Fixed white changed to a white flash every three seconds, 15 April 1913, through an automated acetylene apparatus

No keeper appointed after Cardy's retirement; Coast Guardsmen at the adjacent station assigned to watch the light (LighthouseFriends). The Alcona Historical Society gives 1939 for electrification and automation.
Tender Amaranth grounded on the reef in fog while placing buoys, 31 May 1913; the lifesaving crew assisted
Alcona Historical Society obtained a lease; volunteers restored the buildings in a three-year project
Awarded to the Michigan Department of Natural Resources under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act of 2000; managed by the Alcona Historical Society

keepers.name: Perley Silverthorn
keepers.note: First keeper. Arrived late in 1870 and the first lighting was delayed (LighthouseFriends). Removed 1873; back on the point in 1876 as the first keeper of the Life-Saving Station (LighthouseFriends).

keepers.name: Noah T. Farr
keepers.note: Served for nearly three years before resigning (LighthouseFriends).

keepers.name: John Pasque
keepers.note: Hand injured by a cartridge that exploded, per a local newspaper of 14 September 1877 as quoted by LighthouseFriends. Left in 1882 to head Stannard Rock.

keepers.name: Louis J. Cardy Sr.
keepers.note: The archive gives the dates 1882 to 1913; LighthouseFriends says he served thirty-two years. Died November 1913, aged 81, a few weeks after leaving the station.

wrecks.outcome: Burned in late August 1880 off Alcona (Life-Saving Service, 29 August) or off Sturgeon Point (LighthouseFriends, 28 August). A portion of the Station No. 5 crew picked up five people, the Life-Saving Service gives nine lost, and LighthouseFriends gives twenty lost out of 160 on board. A later dispatch printed by the Cheboygan Northern Tribune said fifty or sixty; the paper said that report proved untrue, and a first-person account in the same issue gives eight missing.
Aground on the reef in fog while placing buoys; the lifesaving crew from the point went out to help, and a tug from Alpena was sent to free her.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The station record gives 1869 (Rowlett) and 1870 (USLHS). The Alcona Historical Society gives spring 1870. LighthouseFriends says the tower was finished in November 1870, and the first lighting was put off until the following spring, which would be 1871. The story reports the spring 1870 and spring 1871 accounts and does not settle the date.

LighthouseFriends and the station record give a third-and-a-half-order lens. The archive's place record gives 'Original Optic Type: SIXTH ORDER, FRESNEL' for 1870. The story uses the third-and-a-half-order lens, which LighthouseFriends describes in detail, and notes the archive's sixth-order entry.

The Life-Saving Service's 1881 report gives 29 August, off Alcona, nine lost. LighthouseFriends gives 28 August, off Sturgeon Point, twenty lost. The Cheboygan Northern Tribune of 4 September 1880 reported a later dispatch that said fifty or sixty lives had been lost, then said that this report proved untrue; a first-person account in the same issue gives eight missing. The Life-Saving Service and LighthouseFriends also differ on the number aboard (110 passengers and 48 crew, against 160). The story gives the dates, the counts and the newspaper's own correction.

LighthouseFriends and the station record give automation in 1913 with the acetylene apparatus and the 1913 Bulletin entry. The Alcona Historical Society gives electrification and automation in 1939, with the last personnel gone in 1941. The story gives both dates.

notes_for_editor: The NRHP nomination (84001370) is not digitised (the NPGallery PDF is a placeholder), so the story has no NRHP source. The 1876 Life-Saving Station is cited through LighthouseFriends and the 1881 report's 'Station No. 5'. The 1881 Life-Saving report is OCR text, and it spells the location 'Alcoua'; quotations are as printed. The Northern Tribune quotations are OCR text as well. The Michigan DNR state-park page (michigan.gov/recsearch/parks/sturgeonpoint) returned HTTP 403, so the DNR's own description was not read. The Alcona page gives the 2026 season hours, which may change; check before publishing. LighthouseFriends' accounts of Silverthorn and Pasque (the 1877 accident, quoted from a local newspaper) and its keeper dates rest on LighthouseFriends alone. The Lighthouse Board reports for 1867 to 1890 are not in the local corpus, so the 1867 appropriation and the 1868 plans are not confirmed in an official report. The Life-Saving Service's 1884 entries about the Sturgeon Point station crew were not used. Cardy's years are given as the archive's dates (1882 to 1913) and LighthouseFriends' thirty-two years. The Life-Saving report's 'Alcoua' is read as Alcona (OCR); the story uses the modern spelling. The Northern Tribune's headline is OCR'd ('DISATSER', 'BUKNED'); the footnote title uses the corrected words. The Alcona page says the lens is no longer in operation, and the story reports that.The 1913 Bulletin item is an excerpt listing illuminant changes, and the story cites it only for the oil-to-acetylene change. No keeper names are withheld; all named keepers are public-service figures from the 1800s and early 1900s. Verification of the 1881 report, the 1880 newspaper, the 1891-92 Light-House Board item and the 1913 Bulletin was against the cached OCR text; no page image was read.
